chapter_theme: Short speeches of the five lands: women waiting through the rains and the cold for men who went far (64-68, 75-77, 79), men praising the girl's body and eyes (62, 70-72), the friend's stratagems and refusals (61, 66, 69, 73, 74), the companion on love's folly (78) and a courtesan's taunt (80).

61.reading: The friend says that, like small boys who cannot ride the little cart a carpenter made yet delight in dragging it by hand, we take our delight in mere kinship with the man of the pond-rich town of good chariots, though we do not enjoy his embrace, and the bangles have grown tight again.
61.nuance: The boys' toy cart is a pleasure taken without its proper use; the friend makes the household's dignity out of a love that has been reduced to a name, and the tightened bangles answer the gossip that she is wasting.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is named by the ponds of the watered town

comparisons.vehicle: தச்சன் செய்த சிறுமா வையம் ஊர்ந்தின் புறாஅர் ஆயினுங் கையின் ஈர்த்தின் புறூஉம் இளையோர் போல
comparisons.tenor: the women, who cannot have his embrace but are content with the bond itself

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; the man is spoken of in the third person, so most likely his messenger

62.reading: The man says that her body, fragrant as a finely made garland of upturned kodal buds, fresh mullai and sweet-petalled kuvalai woven in alternation, is softer than tender shoots and sweet to embrace.
62.nuance: The garland mixes flowers of three lands, hill, woodland and water, so her one body gathers the scents a single landscape cannot give.

thinai_evidence.note: the embrace of lovers is the union of kurinji

comparisons.vehicle: கோடல் எதிர்முகைப் பசுவீ முல்லை நாறிதழ்க் குவளையொ டிடையிடுபு விரைஇ ஐதுதொடை மாண்ட கோதை போல
comparisons.tenor: her body, fragrant with mingled scents
her body, softer than tender shoots

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; he speaks of her in the third person, after their meeting

63.reading: The man asks his heart: you reckon that the work to be done must be pressed hard because there is neither giving nor enjoying for those who have nothing; but will the lovely young woman come along on that work, or will you send me off alone? Tell me.
63.nuance: The heart's argument is the ethic of the giver, that wealth is for giving and enjoying; the man does not deny it but asks the one question it cannot answer, whether she can be taken along.

thinai_evidence.note: the journey for wealth that would part him from her

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the poem names the heart, நெஞ்சே, as addressee

64.reading: The woman says that like a dull-eyed calf that, when the many cows have gone far along the long path, looks at the bare common ground in the evening and cries, we are sick with longing; though he knows it, friend, the man of the far land stays far.
64.nuance: The calf cries at the hour the herds should come home, so the simile carries mullai's own hour of waiting; and அறிந்தும், 'though he knows', puts the fault in his staying, not in his going.

thinai_evidence.note: herds, the village common and evening are the mullai's

comparisons.vehicle: பல்லா நெடுநெறிக் ககன்று வந்தெனப் புன்றலை மன்றம் நோக்கி மாலை மடக்கண் குழவி அலவந் தன்ன
comparisons.tenor: her helpless distress at evening while he stays far off

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names the friend, தோழி, as addressee

65.reading: The woman says the cool rain of dripping drops has come, and the stag that drank the clear water among the hard pebbles is back, frisking with its sweet mate, as if asking those who wait in longing for men who do not return, 'will you stay on, suffering and pained?'

thinai_evidence.note: the arrival of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the rainy season, which comes as though to question the waiting woman

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; she quotes the season's question to those who wait

iraicchi.act: the stag returns to frisk with its sweet mate when the rains come
iraicchi.sense: even the stag keeps the season and comes back to its mate, yet the man who promised has not

66.reading: The friend says the konrai trees with their bent trunks are surely foolish: before the season named by the man who went over the stony path has come, they have taken the stray untimely rain for the rainy season and burst into clustered blooms on every branch.
66.nuance: The friend denies the sign rather than the promise: by calling the trees fools she keeps his word intact, and so the comfort rests on her saying the season has not yet come.

thinai_evidence.note: the konrai's flowering is the sign of the rains

comparisons.tenor: the konrai trees, credited with a fool's mistake

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; she answers the heroine's alarm at the blossoms

67.reading: The woman asks her friend whether they do not think of us, the men who crossed the forest of kalli on scorched land, where the bright neem fruit held in the parrot's curved beak looks like a gold coin that a man with sharp fine nails threads on a new string.
67.nuance: The one bright thing in the burnt land is a gold coin, so the image of the wealth he went for sits in the very scene of his road.

thinai_evidence.note: the scorched land of the kalli forest

comparisons.vehicle: கிள்ளை வளைவாய்க் கொண்ட வேப்ப ஒண்பழம் புதுநாண் நுழைப்பான் நுதிமாண் வள்ளுகிர்ப் பொலங்கல ஒருகா சேய்க்கும்
comparisons.tenor: the yellow neem fruit in the parrot's red beak, like a gold coin being strung

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names the friend, தோழி, as addressee

68.reading: The woman says there is no other medicine for the hard-dewed early winter, when herds of deer eat the ripe old pods of the red-stemmed black gram whose stalks are like the quail's legs, than the chest of the man who embraced us.
68.nuance: The cold is real and the cure is his body: the poem keeps the season's chill and the sickness of absence as one complaint, so 'medicine' needs no metaphor to cover both.

thinai_evidence.note: black-gram fields grazed by deer belong to the woodland, and she waits out the cold

comparisons.tenor: the red stems of the black gram, like a quail's legs

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker

69.reading: The friend tells the man of the slopes, where a lovely female monkey, unable to bear widowhood after her black-eyed leaping mate has died, leaves her untaught young with her kin and leaps from the high ridge to end her life: do not come at midnight, may you live; we suffer.

thinai_evidence.note: hill slopes and midnight

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem addresses the man, சாரல் நாட

ullurai.tenor: the man who risks death on the night path and the girl who would not outlive him

pairs.situation: the man may meet death coming by the dangerous night path
the girl would not survive him
she would end her own life

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses monkeys of the hill slope in a kurinji poem, not leaving its land (porul 7.27)

70.reading: The man says the young girl of the gathered, glossy hair and bright brow is fragrant and cool and a great enchantress; I cannot measure her adornment to say she is such; her few words are soft, and she is soft as a pillow when I embrace her.
70.nuance: 'I cannot say she is such' is the lover's refusal to describe, and then he describes only what touch knows: coolness, fragrance, soft words, a soft body.

thinai_evidence.note: the embrace of union

comparisons.tenor: the girl, who torments like a goddess
her body, soft as a cushion

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; he answers someone who asked what she is like

71.reading: The man says: if medicine, she is medicine; if treasure, she is treasure, the good young daughter of the forest folk of the rocky hills, with budding freckles, lovely broad young breasts, large shoulders and slender waist.
71.nuance: வைப்பு is laid-up wealth: if the poem stands under paalai, as the colophon files it, the praise is an argument against leaving, since the treasure he would go for is already here.

thinai_evidence.note: she is a daughter of the hill-hunters

comparisons.tenor: the girl, who is both the cure and the stored wealth he might seek elsewhere

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; the colophon's paalai suggests he is weighing a journey

72.reading: The man says the large cool eyes of the girl with honeyed words and rounded soft shoulders, who scares the sparrows from the millet sown in the cleared land of the great hill, restless like flowers and like arrows, have caused him a sickness everyone can see.
72.nuance: The girl's work is to drive off small birds with her cries, but it is her eyes that strike; and 'everyone knows' marks the moment his private wound becomes public talk.

thinai_evidence.note: the girl guarding the hill millet from sparrows

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, restless as flowers moving
her eyes, which wound like arrows

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; he explains his visible sickness, likely to his companion

73.reading: The friend tells the woman: you long for your lover's chest; do not despair, may you live; like the Kosar of the single word, who cut down Nannan's fragrant mango tree and drove him from his land, a little hard-eyed scheming is needed.
73.nuance: The scheme is not named: whether it is to withhold meetings so he must marry, or something else, the poem leaves open. மகிழ்நன் for the lover is a marutham word in a poem filed under kurinji.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem names no landscape; the colophon's thinai is kept

comparisons.vehicle: நன்னன் நறுமா கொன்று நாட்டிற் போக்கிய ஒன்று மொழிக் கோசர் போல
comparisons.tenor: the plan the friend proposes to win the lover

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names the friend, தோழி, being addressed by the speaker

74.reading: The friend says that the man of the hill where green bamboo touching the sky springs up with the speed of a horse let loose, not knowing how we pined for him, has himself, they say, wasted like a bull in summer, longing for our fine beauty.
74.nuance: The friend gives the heroine the comfort that the wasting is mutual; the summer bull, a beast of the pasture brought into the hill poem, makes his thinness a matter of season and hunger, the very terms of her own.

thinai_evidence.note: the bamboo hill

comparisons.tenor: the bamboo springing upright with force
the man, wasted with longing as a bull in the dry season

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; she reports what others say of him

75.reading: The woman asks: did you see it yourself, or hear it from someone who saw? Tell us one clear thing, for we long to know; may you win Pataliputra rich in gold, where white-tusked elephants bathe in the Son; from whose mouth did you hear that my lover is coming?
75.nuance: The blessing, may you win Pataliputra, is the richest reward a Tamil poet could name, and it is offered before she knows if the news is true, so her hunger shows in the price she would pay.

thinai_evidence.note: the woman waiting for news of his return

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker; the one who brought news of his coming

76.reading: The woman asks whether they say he will go, the man with a chest like a rock face, of the good land of high hills fenced with kaanthal, in the hard-dewed early winter when the cold north wind sways the big leaves of the taro on the slopes like the ears of a great tusker, and sets us shivering in distress.
76.nuance: The season is the argument: no one should leave in the cold of அச்சிரம், and the shiver she names is both the weather's and her own.

thinai_evidence.note: the news of his going decides it, though the things are of the hill

comparisons.vehicle: சேம்பின் அலங்கல் வள்ளிலை பெருங்களிற்றுச் செவியின் மானத்
comparisons.tenor: the swaying taro leaves, like elephants' ears flapping

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker

77.reading: The woman tells her friend there is no fault in him at all; if fault there is, it is that the broad soft shoulders became easy to leave for the man who went to the hard forest, where in the cruel waste the leaf-heaped cairns of dead travellers give shade to the tall elephant.
77.nuance: She clears him and blames her own shoulders, but the desert of dead men's cairns he chose over them is a reproach she leaves standing; the elephant resting in the shade of graves is the land's indifference to death.

thinai_evidence.note: the cruel waste and the hard forest

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the poem names the friend, தோழி, as addressee

78.reading: The companion tells the man of the shining hill, where the long white waterfall on the great peak resounds like the drum of the skilled old players as it pours down the slope: love is a painful thing; with great folly it goes and stands even by those who do not think it good.
78.nuance: The companion does not blame the girl but love itself, which stands by those who do not value it; the drumming fall frames love as something that pours down unbidden.

thinai_evidence.note: the high hill and its waterfall

thurai_akam.speaker: paangan
thurai_akam.note: the poem addresses the man, இலங்குமலை வெற்ப

79.reading: The woman wonders whether he has stopped in the pretty little hamlet near the desert where a female dove, perched on the swaying dead branch of the scorched-trunked omai whose bark the forest elephant ate with relish, calls with a cry that makes one lonely; he who could leave without a word because of our fault in saying we could not bear it.
79.nuance: She blames herself, தப்பு, for refusing his going, and that refusal is why he went without telling her.

thinai_evidence.note: the desert and its scorched tree

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: addressee inferred: the colophon gives only the speaker

iraicchi.act: the female dove calls for her mate with a lonely cry from the dead branch
iraicchi.sense: the dove near the hamlet where he rests calls its partner as she, alone, calls for him

80.reading: The courtesan says: with whole stalks of water-lily fastened in our hair we will go to bathe at the broad ford where the great flood has come; if she fears that, let her and her kin guard her husband's chest, like the great herds at the front of Ezhini of many spears, who wins fierce wars till the yoke breaks.
80.nuance: The taunt makes the husband a herd of cattle at a war front, property to be guarded against raiders, and herself the raider; the bathing in the flood with lilies is her open claim on him.

thinai_evidence.note: water-lilies and the river flood at the ford

comparisons.tenor: the husband, whom the wife must guard as closely as a war-chief's cattle

links.note: Purananuru 189 concludes that the use of wealth is giving, since king and hunter alike eat one measure; Kuruntokai 63's heart argues the same, that there is no giving and enjoying for the penniless, to drive the man to work.
links.teaches: The puram maxim that wealth exists to be given becomes, in the akam poem, the very reason a man leaves his wife, so the pair shows the giver's ethic carrying a private cost the praise poem never counts.

links.note: Kural 247 takes as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; the heart in Kuruntokai 63 states that premise, and the man answers it only by asking whether she can come along.
links.teaches: Set beside the couplet, the poem shows the Kural's blunt premise as a voice inside a lover's head that he can neither refute nor obey, so the maxim's truth is granted and its price is made visible in the separation.

links.note: In Akananuru 34 the returning man sees a stag feeding and guarding its doe and hurries home; in Kuruntokai 65 the waiting woman sees the stag back with its mate in the rains while her man does not come.
links.teaches: The same sign of the stag with its mate is read from both ends of the separation: for the man it is a spur to return, for the woman it is evidence against him, so the iraicchi's force depends on who is watching.

links.note: Kar Narpathu 4's friend points to the bloomed konrai as the season and the cure of pallor; Kuruntokai 66's friend calls the bloomed konrai foolish, fooled by stray rain, and denies that the season has come.
links.teaches: The friend's comfort can use the konrai either way, as proof the promised season is here or as a false sign to be dismissed, which shows that the consolation lies in the friend's argument and not in the flower itself.

links.note: Perunkoppendu in Purananuru 246 refuses a widow's life and chooses the pyre; the female monkey in Kuruntokai 69, unable to bear widowhood (கைம்மை உய்யா), leaves her young with kin and leaps to her death.
links.teaches: The akam friend borrows the puram queen's refusal of widowhood and gives it to a creature of the hill, making the girl's not outliving her lover a law of nature for the night-visitor to weigh, not a royal vow.

links.note: Kural 1102: other diseases have other cures, but this woman is the cure of the sickness she gives; Kuruntokai 71: if medicine, she is medicine; if treasure, she is treasure.
links.teaches: The man's claim that she is his medicine is the same in both, but the poem adds treasure (வைப்பு), so under its paalai colophon the cure-paradox of the couplet becomes an argument against leaving to seek wealth.

links.note: Both are the man's speech under paalai about leaving for wealth: 63 asks his heart whether she can come along on the work; 71 calls her both medicine and laid-up treasure.
links.teaches: Read in sequence, the two give the man's full answer to the case for earning: 63 asks how wealth helps if it takes him from her, and 71 says she is already the treasure, so the journey has no object.

links.note: Kural 1084: the eyes of this artless girl devour the life of those who see them; Kuruntokai 72: the eyes of the girl scaring sparrows from the millet have, like arrows, made him sick for all to see.
links.teaches: The poem places the couplet's paradox, the simple girl with killing eyes, in her actual work of chasing small birds off the hill millet, and adds what the couplet lacks: the wound is public, known to everyone.

links.note: Akananuru 113 praises the Kosar who never swerve from friendship even in bad times, with unswerving plans (திரிபில் சூழ்ச்சி); Kuruntokai 73 holds up the Kosar of the single word, who cut down Nannan's mango, as the model of hard-eyed scheming (வன்கண் சூழ்ச்சி).
links.teaches: The Kosar's fame was for a kept word carried out by planning, and akam poets drew on it two ways, as loyalty in one poem and as ruthless resolve in the other, so the same people supplied both the virtue and the hard edge of a sworn word.

links.note: Akananuru 265: the woman asks whether the wealth her man went for is as great as the Nandas' treasure hidden at Pataliputra; Kuruntokai 75: the woman wishes the bearer of news of her lover's return to win Pataliputra rich in gold.
links.teaches: Pataliputra's gold was the akam measure of the greatest wealth, and the two women price it against love from opposite sides: one doubts it outweighs her, the other would give it for word of his coming.

links.note: Kural 1236: with bangles and shoulders slackening, what hurts the woman is hearing him called cruel; Kuruntokai 77: there is no fault in him, or if any, it is that her soft shoulders proved easy to leave.
links.teaches: Both women defend the absent man with their wasted shoulders as the evidence, but the poem goes further than the couplet by moving the blame onto those shoulders, while its desert of dead travellers' cairns lets the reproach stand unspoken.

links.note: Purananuru 230: while Ezhini lived, the herds rested in the forest unguarded and safe; Kuruntokai 80: the courtesan tells the wife to guard her husband like the great herds at Ezhini's war front.
links.teaches: The courtesan's taunt rests on Ezhini's puram fame as the protector of herds, so she casts herself as the cattle-raider and the husband as plunder that only a war-chief's watch could keep, using the heroic guard to mock a household one.

source_issues: Kuruntokai colophons give only the speaker (தலைவி கூற்று and the like), so every addressee and stage in thurai_akam is inferred from the poem; each item says so in its note.
75 line 2: தெளிய was repaired from a TSCII leftover (தௌிய); the repair reads correctly.

Thinai differs from the colophon in 68 (mullai: black-gram fields and deer), 71 (kurinji: a hunter's daughter; the colophon's paalai implies a journey the poem does not state), 75 (mullai: waiting for news of his return) and 76 (paalai: his going decides it among hill things).
